item.title: 🔴 How exposure management can help public sector prepare for PHP2Shell-like vulnerabilities
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

PHP2Shell showed how fast a runtime-level flaw can go from disclosure to confirmed exploitation. Here’s how federal, state, local, and education teams can prepare for PHP2Shell-like flaws.

Key takeaways

  1. PHP2Shell went from disclosure to confirmed exploitation within days. With AI shortening the disclosure-to-exploitation window, new critical flaws will likely move just as fast.
  2. Most security teams’ primary challenge with PHP2Shell was knowing where the vulnerabilities were in their environment. Teams that already knew where PHP ran across their IT infrastructure, web applications, and cloud assets were in a position to act quickly.
  3. Initial access flaws will continue to impact your network edge, so work backward from the foothold. Map what an attacker could reach after breaching an edge device, such as root access, management servers, and directory services. Then close those escalation paths by patching kernels and restricting unprivileged user namespaces.
  4. To prioritize, factor in exploitation evidence, not severity alone. Weigh KEV status, exploit prediction scores, and your own internet exposure, as well as pre-approve a plan for systems you can’t patch immediately.

item.title: 🔴 Metasploit Wrap Up: Breaking Zimbra's Identity Boundaries
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

This release we have three pull requests from jburgess-r7 building out coverage for the identity-boundary issues detailed in Rapid7's Breaking Zimbra Identity Boundaries, Part One research.

First up is a new shared mixin, Msf::Exploit::Remote::HTTP::Zimbra, which gives every current and future Zimbra module a common foundation for account/admin SOAP authentication, canonical identity resolution, mailbox-server lookup, and version parsing, allowing future modules to stay focused on the vulnerability instead of re-implementing Zimbra's SOAP plumbing.

Built on top of that mixin are two new modules targeting CVEs from the same research track:

CVE-2026-73571 (#22080) It's an authorization bypass in Zimbra's SaveDraftRequest handling that lets an ordinary authenticated user send mail as another local mailbox without a delegation grant, landing a message in the victim's own Sent folder in the process.

item.title: 🟠 Oracle November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update Addresses 640 CVEs (CVE-2026-114938)
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Oracle addresses 640 CVEs in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update with 655 patches, including 62 critical updates.

Key Takeaways

  1. The November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) contains fixes for 640 unique CVEs in 655 security updates
  2. 62 issues (9.5% of all patches) were assigned a critical severity rating
  3. Oracle Hyperion received the highest number of patches at 267, accounting for 40.8% of all patches

Background

On November 17, Oracle released its Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026. Beginning in May 2026, Oracle introduced CSPUs as a monthly release cycle that sits between the larger quarterly Critical Patch Updates (CPUs), addressing a focused set of high-severity issues on a faster cadence. This CSPU contains fixes for 640 unique CVEs in 655 security updates across 21 Oracle product families. Out of the 655 security updates published, 9.5% of patches were assigned a critical severity.
